facts.claim: SHARE, the user group of IBM computer installations, says of itself that it began in 1955 as the first enterprise IT user group.

facts.claim: In the early mainframe years IBM supplied its software as source code, and SHARE members modified it and exchanged their changes through the SHARE library.
facts.quote: Originally, IBM distributed what software it provided in source form [...] and systems programmers commonly made small local additions or modifications and exchanged them with other users.

source.title: SHARE (computing)

facts.note: Encyclopaedia entry used as a last resort: no primary SHARE or IBM document on the library could be fetched. The date is the founding year of SHARE, not of a particular exchange.

facts.claim: Dennis Ritchie dates the birth of Unix at Bell Labs to 1969, five years before the first paper describing it.

facts.claim: Richard Stallman recalls joining the MIT Artificial Intelligence Lab in 1971 and finding a community in which sharing software was the normal practice.
facts.quote: I became part of a software-sharing community that had existed for many years. Sharing of software was not limited to our particular community; it is as old as computers, just as sharing of recipes is as old as cooking.

source.title: The GNU Project
source.author: Richard Stallman

facts.note: This is Stallman's own later recollection (essay first published in 1998), not a document from 1971.

facts.claim: In February 1976 Bill Gates wrote an open letter accusing computer hobbyists of stealing software, setting out the case that software should be paid for rather than shared.
facts.quote: As the majority of hobbyists must be aware, most of you steal your software. Hardware must be paid for, but software is something to share. Who cares if the people who worked on it get paid?

source.author: William Henry Gates III

facts.note: Quoted from the Wikisource transcription of the letter, which is dated February 3, 1976 in the text.

facts.claim: Bill Joy assembled the first Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) at the University of California, Berkeley, early in 1977.
facts.quote: Early in 1977, Joy put together the "Berkeley Software Distribution."

source.title: Twenty Years of Berkeley Unix: From AT&T-Owned to Freely Redistributable (in Open Sources: Voices from the Open Source Revolution)
source.author: Marshall Kirk McKusick

facts.note: The account is by Marshall Kirk McKusick, a member of the Berkeley group, written in 1999.

facts.claim: On 27 September 1983 Richard Stallman announced on Usenet that he would write a complete Unix-compatible system called GNU and give it away.
facts.quote: Starting this Thanksgiving I am going to write a complete Unix-compatible software system called GNU (for Gnu's Not Unix)

source.title: Initial Announcement (new Unix implementation)
source.author: Richard Stallman

facts.note: The GNU Project page that hosts the text states that it was "posted by Richard Stallman on September 27, 1983". gnu.org was reachable only over http from this machine.

facts.claim: Stallman gave an ethical reason for GNU: he held that sharing programs is a duty and refused to sign nondisclosure or software licence agreements.
facts.quote: I consider that the golden rule requires that if I like a program I must share it with other people who like it. I cannot in good conscience sign a nondisclosure agreement or a software license agreement.

source.title: Initial Announcement (new Unix implementation)
source.author: Richard Stallman

facts.claim: The GNU Manifesto of 1985 set out the rule that later became copyleft: anyone may modify and redistribute GNU, but nobody may restrict its further redistribution.

facts.claim: Stallman describes copyleft, the method behind the GNU General Public License, as using copyright law to keep a program free.

source.title: The GNU Project
source.author: Richard Stallman

facts.note: The explanation is from Stallman's 1998 essay; it is dated here to the first GPL (1989), the licence that implements it.

facts.claim: Version 1 of the GNU General Public License, dated February 1989, states its purpose as guaranteeing the freedom to share and change free software.
facts.quote: our General Public License is intended to guarantee your freedom to share and change free software--to make sure the software is free for all its users.

source.title: GNU General Public License, version 1

facts.claim: In June 1989 Berkeley released Networking Release 1, its first freely redistributable code.

facts.note: Her account was written on 2 January 2006 and published on Opensource.com in February 2018.

disputed.what: The date of the meeting at which "open source" was adopted

facts.claim: In Peterson's account the term was adopted at a strategy meeting at VA Research on 5 February 1998, where Todd Anderson put it forward and Eric Raymond endorsed it.
facts.quote: Later that week, on February 5, 1998, a group was assembled at VA Research to brainstorm on strategy. [...] Todd advocated the "open source" model, and Eric endorsed this.

source.author: Christine Peterson

facts.note: The date is contested between the sources. Peterson's narrative says 5 February 1998, and Raymond's call of 8 February 1998 also points to 5 February; the Open Source Initiative's history says 3 February 1998, and the editor's introduction to Peterson's own article calls 3 February the anniversary.

disputed.what: The date of the meeting at which "open source" was adopted

positions.says: The key meeting was on 5 February 1998 at VA Research.
The label was created at a strategy session on 3 February 1998 in Palo Alto.
The brainstorm was the day after his meeting with Netscape, which he dates elsewhere to 4 February.

facts.claim: On 8 February 1998 Eric Raymond publicly called on the community to replace the term "free software" with "open source", saying the group had come up with the label together.
facts.quote: I brainstormed this with some Silicon Valley fans of Linux (including Larry Augustin of the Linux International board of directors) the day after my meeting with Netscape (Feb 5th). We kicked around and discarded several alternatives, and we came up with a replacement label we all liked: "open source".

source.title: Goodbye, "free software"; hello, "open source"
source.author: Eric S. Raymond

facts.note: Raymond writes "we came up with"; he does not name Peterson in this passage. The date of 8 February is from his own preface to the document.

facts.claim: Raymond's stated reason for the new label was pragmatic: "free software" was ambiguous and made business people nervous.
facts.quote: Second, the term makes a lot of corporate types nervous. While this does not intrinsically bother me in the least, we now have a pragmatic interest in converting these people rather than thumbing our noses at them.

source.author: Eric S. Raymond

facts.note: The words were said in an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times published on 1 June 2001. No transcript is known, so the newspaper is the record of the words and The Register is a second-hand record.

facts.claim: Ballmer's explanation of the remark was about licensing: he said that using any open source software obliges a company to make the rest of its software open source.

source.title: Ballmer: 'Linux is a cancer'
source.author: Thomas C. Greene

facts.claim: The remark is usually repeated in the short form "Linux is a cancer", which is the headline The Register gave its report, and which drops the qualifier about intellectual property.
facts.quote: Ballmer: 'Linux is a cancer'

source.title: Ballmer: 'Linux is a cancer'
source.author: Thomas C. Greene

facts.note: The short form is a headline, not the sentence Ballmer is reported to have said. The fuller sentence, as The Register quotes it, is "Linux is a cancer that attaches itself in an intellectual property sense to everything it touches".

facts.claim: GitHub reported for 2024 more than 5.2 billion contributions to more than 518 million projects, a figure that mixes open source, public and private work.
facts.quote: In 2024, developers around the world made more than 5.2 billion contributions to more than 518 million open source, public, and private projects.

source.title: Octoverse: AI leads Python to top language as the number of global developers surges
source.author: GitHub Staff

facts.note: GitHub's own figures; they cover private projects as well and are not a measure of open source alone.

facts.claim: The Software Freedom Conservancy's Bradley Kuhn criticised the definition for not requiring public disclosure of training sets, and said the OSI should not have published it yet.
facts.quote: the OSAID fails to require reproducibility by the public of the scientific process of building these systems, because the OSAID fails to place sufficient requirements on the licensing and public disclosure of training sets

source.title: Open Source AI Definition Erodes the Meaning of "Open Source"
source.author: Bradley M. Kuhn

facts.claim: The European Union's Cyber Resilience Act entered into force on 10 December 2024, with its main obligations applying from 11 December 2027.
facts.quote: The CRA entered into force on 10 December 2024. The main obligations introduced by the Act will apply from 11 December 2027, with reporting obligations to apply as of 11 September 2026.

source.title: Cyber Resilience Act

facts.claim: The Act creates a new legal category, the open source software steward, for bodies that sustain open source products used commercially, under a lighter regime than manufacturers.
facts.quote: the novel legal category of open-source software stewards is introduced. These are legal persons who provide support on a sustained basis for the development of such products which are intended for commercial activities, and who play a main role in ensuring their viability, and are subject to a light-touch and tailor-made regulatory regime.

source.title: The Cyber Resilience Act and open source

facts.note: From the European Commission's explanatory page. The text of the Regulation on EUR-Lex returned a 202 challenge page and could not be read with the fetch tool.

facts.claim: The Commission says only open source software supplied in the course of a commercial activity falls within the Act.
facts.quote: only free and open-source software that is made available on the market, and therefore supplied for distribution or use in the course of a commercial activity, falls in scope of the Cyber Resilience Act.

source.title: The Cyber Resilience Act and open source

facts.claim: On 1 May 2025 Redis added the OSI-approved AGPL as a licence option from Redis 8.
facts.quote: Adding the OSI-approved AGPL as an additional licensing option for Redis, starting with Redis 8 (available now);

source.title: Redis is now available under the AGPLv3 open source license
source.author: Rowan Trollope

facts.claim: Redis wrote in the same post that the SSPL is not truly open source.
facts.quote: SSPL is not truly open source because the Open Source Initiative clarified it lacks the requisites to be an OSI-approved license.

source.title: Redis is now available under the AGPLv3 open source license
source.author: Rowan Trollope

facts.note: The same post says that AWS and Google "now maintain their own fork" and that "the change hurt our relationship with the Redis community". The author is Rowan Trollope, writing for Redis.

facts.claim: On 19 May 2025 Microsoft released the Windows Subsystem for Linux as open source.
facts.quote: Today we’re very excited to announce the open-source release of the Windows Subsystem for Linux.

source.title: The Windows Subsystem for Linux is now open source
source.author: Pierre Boulay

facts.claim: GitHub reported in October 2025 that more than 180 million developers use the platform, 36 million of whom joined in the past year.
facts.quote: Every second, more than one new developer on average joined GitHub—over 36 million in the past year. It’s our fastest absolute growth rate yet and 180 million-plus developers now work and build on GitHub.

source.title: Octoverse: A new developer joins GitHub every second as AI leads TypeScript to #1
source.author: GitHub Staff

facts.note: GitHub's own figures for accounts on its platform.

facts.claim: JUnit 4 is distributed under the Eclipse Public License, an open source licence.
facts.quote: THE ACCOMPANYING PROGRAM IS PROVIDED UNDER THE TERMS OF THIS ECLIPSE PUBLIC LICENSE ("AGREEMENT").

source.title: JUnit 4 licence file (Eclipse Public License 1.0)

facts.note: The licence file of the current JUnit 4 repository; it does not show which licence the 1997 version carried. The file is undated, so the fact is dated to the year it was read.

facts.claim: Cunningham's later project, the Smallest Federated Wiki, is published on GitHub under the MIT licence or the GPL version 2.
facts.quote: You may use the Smallest Federated Wiki under either the

source.title: Smallest Federated Wiki: ReadMe
source.author: Ward Cunningham and contributors

facts.note: The sentence continues with links to the "MIT License" or the "GNU General Public License" "(GPL) Version 2". The ReadMe carries no date and GitHub's API refused the request for the repository's creation date, so the fact is dated to the year it was read; the project is older.
